questions.title: How can fair use be decided on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without a factual record?
questions.question_body: In Santos v. Kimmel, the Second Circuit affirms dismissal of the copyright infringement claim at the pleading stage, stating that fair use may be "so clearly established by a complaint as to support dismissal." But fair use involves a four-factor test that seems fact-intensive—transformative use, nature of the work, amount used, and market harm all seem to require evidence. How can a court evaluate these factors when all it has is the complaint? Is there something special about fair use that makes it different from other affirmative defenses at the motion-to-dismiss stage? When is it appropriate to dismiss on fair use grounds versus letting it go to discovery?

questions.title: Why does the "reasonable observer" standard control transformative use instead of the creator's intent?
questions.question_body: Santos argues that Kimmel "instigated the creation" of the Cameo videos and is therefore the "designer" of their original purpose, making Kimmel's use non-transformative. The court rejects this, citing Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith for the principle that "the subjective intent of the user... [does not] determine the purpose of the use." Instead, the court applies a "reasonable observer" standard. I'm confused: Santos says the videos were meant to convey "hope, strength, perseverance," while Kimmel used them to mock Santos's willingness to "say absurd things for money." Why does the reasonable observer's perception of the secondary use matter more than either party's intent? What is the theoretical justification for this objective standard in transformative use analysis?

questions.title: What happened to the good faith requirement for fair use after Harper & Row?
questions.question_body: Santos argues that Kimmel's use of fictitious names to request the Cameo videos constitutes bad faith, which should negate the fair use defense, citing Harper & Row's statement that "fair use presupposes good faith and fair dealing." The Second Circuit says the Supreme Court has "since distanced itself from this statement" but doesn't cite specific cases showing how. What cases retreated from the good faith requirement? Is bad faith now completely irrelevant to fair use, or does it still matter in some circumstances? The court seems to reframe the inquiry as whether the use "supplants" the copyright holder's rights—is that now the operative test instead of good faith?

questions.title: Why did the Second Circuit avoid the copyright preemption issue and decide contract claims on state law grounds instead?
questions.question_body: The district court dismissed Santos's breach of contract and breach of implied contract claims as preempted by the Copyright Act. On appeal, Santos argues these claims are "qualitatively different from a copyright infringement claim" and thus not preempted. The Second Circuit says it "need not resolve this issue" because the claims fail under state law anyway. What principle allows the court to affirm on alternative grounds without reaching the preemption question? Is this avoidance discretionary? Are there situations where a court must address preemption before reaching the merits of the state law claim?

questions.title: How does the third-party beneficiary analysis work when some contract provisions have express third-party language but others don't?
questions.question_body: Santos tries to enforce the Cameo Terms of Service as a third-party beneficiary, but the court applies Illinois law's "strong presumption against conferring benefits to noncontracting third parties." The court notes that other provisions of the Terms of Service "do contain third-party beneficiary language," suggesting that when the parties wanted third parties to enforce provisions, they said so expressly—and the absence of such language in the provisions Santos relies on means he can't enforce them. Is this a recognized canon of contract interpretation? How does this negative inference interact with the requirement that the implication must be "so strong as to be practically an express declaration"?

questions.title: Why doesn't performing services in reliance on fraud constitute "out-of-pocket loss" under New York law?
questions.question_body: Santos's fraudulent inducement claim was dismissed because he failed to allege "out-of-pocket loss" as required under New York law. But Santos created and delivered personalized videos based on Kimmel's false representations about who he was and the intended use. He gave something of value—his performance and likeness—based on the fraud. Why doesn't providing the videos constitute an out-of-pocket loss? Is it because he was paid through Cameo? Would the difference between what he was paid and what he would have charged had he known the true purpose qualify as out-of-pocket loss?

questions.title: How does the fourth fair use factor distinguish between "damaging" a market and "usurping" it?
questions.question_body: The court quotes Hachette Book Group for the principle that the fourth fair use factor asks "not whether the second work would damage the market for the first (by, for example, devaluing it through parody or criticism), but whether it usurps the market for the first by offering a competing substitute." I'm struggling with this distinction. If Kimmel's segments made Santos's original videos less valuable by mocking them, why isn't that market harm? The court also cites Campbell v. Acuff-Rose for the idea that creators won't license "critical reviews or lampoons of their own productions"—does this mean parody and criticism can essentially never cause cognizable market harm under the fourth factor?
